subject: End-to-end test of the context layer, and the integration bugs it found (#58)
task:
End-to-end test of the context layer, and the integration bugs it found (#58)

tests/test_e2e.py runs the whole path on two small repositories with history:
ingest the record (git + markdown), sync the code graph across both, index code
and record for retrieval, then call context, impact, search, read and
file_history over MCP on a sample change. It checks that every cited id reads
back, the blast radius crosses into the other repository, answers fit their
budgets, and a repeated call is served from the cache with the same tokens.
No model, no network, hash embedder; about 10 s.

Fixed along the way (orion/agent.py unless noted):
- Without an orion.yaml the tools never saw the code graph that
  `orion codegraph sync --repo` writes to .orion/graph.duckdb. They now open it
  for each call (and close it, so a sync can still write).
- A server held the retrieval index open read-only for its whole life, which
  DuckDB treats as a lock: `orion rag index` failed while any session was open.
  The index now closes 5 s after the last call; the embedding model is kept.
- The code graph was queried without the checkout's repository, so a path or
  name could resolve in another repo; its unresolved notes came out as dict
  reprs; files it covers were listed twice (graph edge and text-match import).
- read of a symbol:/file:/route: id returned the platform store's generic asset
  view instead of the code graph's dependants and dependencies.
- One document could fill several slots with its chunks, and the same passage
  came back twice when both the record section index and the retrieval index
  held it. One passage per document now, and near-identical passages merge.
- A code-graph-only store no longer counts as a data platform.
- store.py: .orion/ gets a .gitignore, so Orion's own files never show up as
  part of a change (they did, in impact with a base ref).

task:

* Review: resolve an import of a changed name to the module it names

from other.http import fetch, a relative import from another package,
import { fetch } from "./http" in a different directory, and
use crate::other::fetch no longer count as importing the changed
definition: the reference is scoped imports_other and reaches the model
as a fact instead of the deterministic finding. Relative imports are
resolved against the importing file; absolute ones match by trailing
segments since the import root is not known.

* Symbol references: a wildcard import of the changed module links its uses

from app.http import * and use crate::http::* bind the name when they
resolve to the definition's module, so a bare call in such a file is a
linked reference. Carried over from the last self-review round on #11.

* Symbol references: a definition in a package file is imported by the package's name

app/__init__.py, lib/index.ts and http/mod.rs stand for their directory,
so from app import fetch and import { fetch } from "./lib" resolve to
them. Raised by Orion's own review of #13.

* Symbol references: an import that names no module keeps counting as an import of the symbol

A file whose binding import cannot be resolved (Go, Ruby, or a shape the
parser does not handle) is scoped imports_it even when another import in
the same file resolves elsewhere. Raised by Orion's own review of #13.

* README: say how imports are resolved

* Symbol references: Rust super and self resolve against the importing file's own module

`use super::x` and `use self::x` now resolve relative to the module the
importing file belongs to (a file is its own module; mod.rs stands for its
directory), instead of the file's parent directory.

* Symbol references: wildcard imports are checked before an import from elsewhere settles the scope; `import x as name` names module x

A file with `from other import fetch` and `from app.http import *` may
rebind fetch to ours, so the wildcard source is resolved before the named
import from elsewhere demotes the file to imports_other. A Python
`import x as fetch` now carries module x as its source instead of counting
as an unsourced (fail-open) import of fetch.

* Symbol references: `import x as name` binds a module, not a name from one

A plain import aliased to the symbol's name is no longer an import of the
symbol. Calls through the alias (`fetch.fetch()` after `import app.http
as fetch`) are still linked via the module-qualified path.

subject: Verify every database connection against Supabase's pinned root
task:
Verify every database connection against Supabase's pinned root

Until now every connection this project made used psycopg's default
sslmode=prefer: encrypted, never authenticated. Nothing noticed for the whole
life of the project; a Node client refused the pooler's chain in the Paddock
parity gate, which is the only reason it surfaced (docs/paddock-gate.md).

store/connect.py is now the one place a connection is opened. Sixteen
psycopg.connect call sites across twelve files go through it, and it sets
sslmode=verify-full and sslrootcert=store/supabase-ca.pem as keyword arguments,
which psycopg applies over anything in the conninfo -- so neither a connection
string nor an environment variable can downgrade it. A missing CA file refuses
to connect rather than connecting unverified: silent-and-consequential is the
one failure shape the baseline forbids, and here it would be silent in exactly
the way it already was.

The root is Supabase's own ("Supabase Root 2021 CA", SHA-256 80:70:25:AD:...),
taken from the pooler's handshake -- trust-on-first-use; cross-check against
the dashboard's downloadable CA.

Tests, deny-side first: the same host and credentials against a genuine but
unrelated self-signed root (tests/fixtures/unrelated-root.pem, made with
openssl) fail the handshake with a certificate error. Only then is the pinned
root shown to be accepted, with libpq's own ssl_in_use on the client
connection. pg_stat_ssl was the wrong instrument: Supavisor terminates TLS, so
the backend's row describes the pooler's internal hop and reads false even when
the client hop is verified -- the first version of the test asserted that and
failed for the right reason. 151 tests.

subject: Require a bearer key on every data route
task:
Require a bearer key on every data route

The corpus holds client-shaped material and named people behind /repos,
/search and /ask, which until now anyone reaching the port could read. The
three data routes now take `Authorization: Bearer <STUDBOOK_API_KEY>`; /healthz
(counts and model names, nothing from the record) and the static shell at /
stay open, and the page can fetch nothing until a key is entered.

What the design refuses to do, and why:

  - It does not fall back to "no auth" when the key is unset. The server
    refuses to start, before loading models, with a message that says how to
    generate one. A failure that is silent and consequential is the one shape
    the security baseline forbids, and "runs fine, just open" is exactly that.
  - It does not say which part was wrong. Missing header, wrong scheme and
    wrong key get one 401 with one detail and a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
    challenge; the comparison is constant-time.
  - It does not validate the body first. The key is checked before the 422s,
    so an unauthenticated caller cannot learn the request schema.
  - The page keeps the key in sessionStorage -- gone with the tab, never
    persisted -- and every storage access is guarded for private windows.

Tests are deny-side first: the startup refusal is asserted as a raise, every
data route is asserted 401 without a key with no passage text in the body, and
only then are the admit-side cases run under a dedicated test key so the suite
never depends on the operator's real one. The .env.example entry and the M5
write-up record the scope honestly: one shared key is right for one operator on
localhost; more than one caller needs identity, rate limiting and an audit log,
none of which this is. 146 tests.

subject: Pin the generator's sampling, then halve over-refusal

Two findings, the second only visible once the first was fixed.

1. Generation ran at the API default temperature. For a tool whose product
is a citation that is wrong on its own terms -- the same question against the
same passages could come back with different receipts -- and it made the
instrument noisy: two runs of the same dev split disagreed by 0.175 correctness
and five over-refusals, none of it signal. Pinning it turned up three things,
none of them expected:

  - anthropic 1.6.0 removed `temperature` from Messages.create()'s signature;
    passing it raises TypeError. It goes through extra_body instead.
  - It is honoured -- verified, not assumed: three samples of a high-entropy
    prompt came back identical at 0 and all different at the default.
  - It is model-dependent. Haiku 4.5 takes it; Sonnet 5 answers 400
    `"temperature" is deprecated for this model`. So answers are reproducible
    and judge verdicts are not, and judge.py says so instead of pretending.
    generate_answer retries once without it and prints that answers from that
    model are no longer reproducible.

The TypeError passed every existing test, because they all use a fake client
that accepts any keyword, and surfaced 40 questions into a paid run. A test now
binds the request we build against the installed SDK's real signature.
Determinism is reduced, not absolute: one of three answers still differed in
wording on a re-run, with identical scores.

2. M4 called over-refusal the largest lever left and diagnosed it from a sample
of six. run_generation --dump now records every answer, verdict and where a gold
passage landed, and eval/diagnose.py splits refusals into retrieval (nothing
gold was retrieved -- refusing was right) and generation (it had the passage and
refused anyway). Exhaustively: 11 of 34 answerable dev questions refused, 7 with
the gold passage in front of them, from three distinct causes. The prompt now
answers a "this change" ambiguity for both changes instead of refusing, permits
one cited inferential step marked as inference, and bans the self-contradicting
refusal -- wh-06 quoted the rationale from [1] and then called it absent. A
fourth clause follows from the trap audit: a passage recording that something
does not exist is an answer, cited as normal, not a refusal.

  dev, pinned:  correctness 1.30 -> 1.50, fully correct 0.60 -> 0.70,

                faithfulness 0.95 -> 0.90.

subject: Detect a WebSocket disconnect immediately, not only via a failed send
task:
Detect a WebSocket disconnect immediately, not only via a failed send

Task 7's own review traced through uvicorn's real behavior: the poll loop
only ever learned of a disconnect as a side effect of a later failed
send(), and a send only happens when last_seq has actually advanced. A
client that disconnects during a quiet stretch -- no new events, so no
send ever attempted -- left the server-side task polling the database
every 2s forever, an unbounded per-connection resource leak. The existing
test suite couldn't catch this because Starlette's TestClient force-
cancels the server-side task on disconnect regardless of app behavior, a
test-only artifact with no production equivalent.

_sleep_or_disconnect races receive() against the poll sleep so a
disconnect message ends the wait immediately. Tested directly against the
extracted helper (a _Receivable Protocol, narrower than WebSocket, so a
fake stand-in can exercise it without a real ASGI connection) rather than
through the full route, sidestepping the TestClient masking issue
entirely. Mutation-tested: reverted to the original bare-sleep behavior,
confirmed the new disconnect test times out exactly as the bug predicts,
reverted back.

subject: Fix C2-R6: clamp the reducing reference to the sleeve's realized position
task:
Fix C2-R6: clamp the reducing reference to the sleeve's realized position

Round 4 asked `is_reducing` about `position_qty + working_qty`. Only the first
half is realized -- `working_qty` is a prediction about orders that can still be
cancelled. A separately-charged fill in the same symbol can carry `position_qty`
through zero without touching a stale working entry, after which the two point
the SAME way and their sum exceeds anything the sleeve holds. An order sized to
that inflated figure was classified "purely position-reducing" while opening
brand-new, entirely unreserved exposure: four orders and zero denials put $5,000
on a $1,000 allocation, a five-order variant breached at a realistic 10%
fat-finger band, and a HALTED sleeve was approved for an order that added
exposure -- the exact outcome round 4's own carve-out ruling said it would never
permit.

New `SleeveAccount.reducing_reference_qty()` clamps the combination into the
closed interval between zero and the realized position, so a still-working
reduction can only ever shrink the allowance toward zero, never grow it or flip
its sign. It is the single accessor `reserve()`, `_check_sleeve_capital` and
`_check_sleeve_halted` all consume -- three hand-written copies of the same
expression drifting apart is the root cause this chain kept re-discovering.

Verified by execution against every repro in the round-4 re-review (all four now
denied or correctly charged), against C2-R4's two-close repro and the round-4
brief's partial-fill scenario (both unchanged), and against round 2/3's five
regression scenarios plus cross-sleeve leakage. Seven independent mutations of
the new code are each caught by a named test, including the re-review's V5
(`_check_sleeve_halted` reading `position_qty` alone), which previously survived
the entire suite.

C2-R5 is untouched by this commit and remains open; see the next one.

task:
Phase 5.4: live websocket source with transport and data watchdogs

LiveDataSource wraps an injected websocket-shaped transport with two independent
watchdogs: transport_stale() catches a dead socket (no frame, heartbeat or bar,
within 3x the heartbeat interval); stale_symbols() catches a healthy socket

backoff -> re-auth -> re-subscribe-full-symbol-list -> REST-backfill -> upsert
sequence, upserting idempotently via BarStore so overlapping backfill windows
never duplicate.

`stream` (the injected transport) and `stream()` (the DataSource Protocol method)
can't both be plain attribute/method on one instance -- Python only has one
namespace slot for the name. Resolved with a small _TransportHandle facade that
is both callable (drives the real watchdog-updating pump) and attribute-
forwarding (so `source.stream.subscribed` still reaches the wrapped transport
directly, per the plan's own verbatim test). Verified structurally sound under
mypy --strict via an added test that uses LiveDataSource through a `DataSource`-
typed variable.

subject: Fix C2: sleeve capital tracks net exposure, not lifetime gross-traded volume
task:
Fix C2: sleeve capital tracks net exposure, not lifetime gross-traded volume

_check_sleeve_capital computed projected = committed_notional + qty*price
regardless of side -- a SELL that closes an existing long added its full
notional to projected exactly like a BUY opening new exposure, so a
fully-committed sleeve could never get flat, violating CLAUDE.md invariant
5's "you can still get flat, you cannot dig deeper" for the exact case it
exists to protect. SleeveAccount.apply_fill() had the same bug: it only ever
accumulated fill_notional, with no path to reduce it when a fill closes
exposure.

Both now evaluate exposure DELTA -- (abs(resulting_qty) - abs(existing_qty))
* price -- instead of gross notional:

- SleeveFill gains symbol/side fields so a fill can be netted against the
  sleeve's own existing position in that symbol; SleeveAccount tracks
  per-symbol net qty and apply_fill's filled_notional now moves by the
  signed exposure delta (negative when reducing, equal to the full fill
  notional when opening fresh from flat -- a strict generalization, not a
  behavior change for any position opened from flat, verified by hand
  against the existing partial-fill tests and confirmed passing unchanged).
- RiskEngine gains a shared _resulting_position_qty helper (used by both
  _check_position_limit, pure refactor, and _check_sleeve_capital) and
  _check_sleeve_capital now projects committed_notional + exposure_delta
  against the allocation. .reserve() intentionally stays gross-notional
  (conservative, documented scope limitation: over-counts a still-working
  reducing order until it fills, the safe direction of error).

New tests: a fully-committed sleeve's SleeveAccount returns to full headroom
after a fully-closing fill; an adding fill counts only its incremental
delta; RiskEngine approves a reducing SELL that closes a fully-committed
position in both ACTIVE and REDUCING state; a SELL with no existing position
(a new short) is still correctly denied.

Also I1: strengthens test_risk_properties.py's
test_no_sequence_of_approved_orders_can_breach_a_sleeve_allocation, which
previously reserved-and-fully-filled every approved order in the same step,

equivalent committed_notional property: mutation-testing (mutating
committed_notional to filled_notional-only, as required) found that
asserting via the composite property does NOT catch that mutation even with
the strengthened sequence, because RiskEngine._check_sleeve_capital reads
that same property to gate approvals, making it self-consistently satisfied

silently invalidates the validation -- only re-deriving the fingerprint at

the new gate_results table close it. evaluate_gate itself is deliberately
left untouched -- persisting a GateResult is a separate, deliberate act, not
a side effect of every exploratory gate evaluation, and auto-wiring it would
also make research/ depend on risk/, reversing this codebase's layering.

Phase 4.1 fix: SleeveAccount.apply_fill handles partial fills correctly

apply_fill() released a reservation's entire notional the instant any fill
arrived, including a partial one, silently understating committed_notional
for the still-outstanding unfilled portion -- a capital-cap bypass reached
via fill granularity rather than order count. Now a fill reduces the
remaining reservation by its own real notional (qty * price), clamped at

task:
Fix I4: multi-symbol backtests crash in Portfolio.mark

run_backtest marked with {bar.symbol: bar.close}, a single-entry dict
containing only the current bar's symbol. On an interleaved multi-symbol bar
stream, the symbol not in the current bar is exactly the previously-filled
position the portfolio is still holding, so Portfolio.mark's fail-loud

HistoricalDataSource(symbols=[...]) and run_backtest both already treat
multi-symbol streams as first-class.

Now tracks the last-seen close per symbol across the whole bar stream and
marks against that accumulated dict, preserving the fail-loud guarantee for
a symbol the stream has genuinely never sent a bar for.

both and holds; confirmed it reproduces the exact ValueError (on the first
bar marked after both positions are open) before the fix, and that the final
equity curve's positions_value reflects both positions after it.

subject: Fix I2: the -inf sentinel is not valid JSON, Postgres will reject it
task:
Fix I2: the -inf sentinel is not valid JSON, Postgres will reject it

_INSUFFICIENT_DATA_SHARPE (float("-inf")) was written straight into
research_trials.metrics, a JSON column. -Infinity is not a legal JSON number
under RFC 8259; SQLite's permissive JSON1 extension (every test here runs
against sqlite:///:memory:) accepts it, Postgres's stricter JSON/JSONB parser
does not.

TrialLog.record now sanitizes non-finite metric values to JSON null before
the insert (_json_safe_metrics), and _row_to_trial_record reverses null back
to -inf on read (_floats_from_json_safe) -- the only non-finite value this
codebase ever produces, so the reversal is unambiguous. TrialRecord.metrics's
Python-side type and every existing comparison stay exactly -inf/float; only
the on-disk representation changes.

No Postgres is provisioned in this environment, so this is verified at the
string level: a new test confirms the raw stored row (queried directly,
bypassing TrialLog's own read-path reversal) has None where -inf was logged,
and that re-serializing it contains neither "Infinity" nor "NaN" -- the
literal tokens Postgres's parser would reject. A live-Postgres round-trip
test is deferred until Postgres is provisioned (Phase 4/5 or CI), consistent
with every other persistence module in this codebase being SQLite-only-tested
today, not a new gap.

subject: Phase 3.7: synthetic controls -- the harness is proven on known answers
task:
Phase 3.7: synthetic controls -- the harness is proven on known answers

Extends shu.research.synthetic's noise_bars/trending_bars with an additive,
keyword-only bar_spacing parameter (default timedelta(minutes=1), zero
behavior change for every existing caller -- confirmed via zero regressions
on test_synthetic.py's full 7-test suite before and after). Daily spacing
(bar_spacing=timedelta(days=1)) is what tests/unit/test_validation_controls.py
uses: at the brief's literal n=3000 one-minute bars (~8 trading days), the
gate's min_backtest_length check cannot clear its own bar at any n_trials
these tests produce, making the positive control mathematically impossible
to pass regardless of injected edge size, since GateResult.passed is a
conjunction of all six checks. One bar per UTC calendar day is a direct fit
to daily_returns()'s day-bucketing convention and keeps evaluate_gate's
~20-30 internal backtest executions per call fast.

Three controls, each with a predetermined correct verdict:
- Negative control: MovingAverageCrossover against pure noise fails the gate
  (n=700 daily bars, seed=101) -- confirmed: 4 of 6 checks fail as expected,
  only min_trades and min_backtest_length pass (pure sample-size checks,
  unrelated to whether the edge is real).
- Positive control: MovingAverageCrossover against noise plus an injected
  drift passes the gate (n=800 daily bars, seed=202, edge_bps_per_bar=3) --
  all six checks pass with margin (e.g. min_trades observed=45 vs
  threshold=30, deflated_sharpe observed=1.00 vs threshold=0.50).
- Overfit control: the best of 60 noise configurations still fails
  specifically on deflated_sharpe (n=1700 daily bars, seed=303) --
  confirmed: deflated_sharpe observed=0.1966 vs threshold=0.50, alongside
  three other checks failing too (walk_forward_efficiency, pbo,
  min_backtest_length), consistent with this being pure noise throughout.

Positive control tuning, per this task's explicit instruction to raise the
edge and investigate rather than weaken a threshold: raising edge_bps_per_bar
alone (tried 1/2/3/5/8/15/25/40 at n=150) was insufficient -- and, at the
higher end, actively counterproductive. MovingAverageCrossover(5,15) only
trades on an SMA crossover, and a larger edge produces a *cleaner* trend
that crosses the two SMAs *fewer* times: at edge_bps_per_bar=15/25/40 the
strategy buys once and holds for the whole dataset (min_trades observed=1.0
against a threshold of 30, every time, regardless of how much larger the
edge got from there). Multiple crossovers need the noise (a fixed +-0.25
absolute range, independent of price or edge) to stay comparable to the
per-bar drift long enough to whipsaw the SMAs repeatedly -- antagonistic to
a single large edge. The reconciling combination, found by sweeping both
edge and dataset length and confirmed robust across n=700..900 at this edge
(not a knife-edge coincidence of one bar count): edge_bps_per_bar=3 with
n=800, comfortably clearing every check. No GateThresholds value and no
check's logic were touched -- only the injected synthetic drift's size and
the synthetic dataset's length, exactly the class of adjustment this task
authorized.

Full quality gate: 230 unit tests pass (227 baseline + 3 new), mypy --strict
clean (46 src files), ruff check + format clean, both custom lints clean
(lint_strategy_purity.py unaffected; lint_docstrings.py's one violation in
test_clock.py predates this change), bandit clean on src (one pre-existing
Low finding in synthetic.py's random.Random usage, already flagged
`# noqa: S311` since Task 5 and untouched by this diff).

subject: Phase 3.5: strategy and dataset fingerprinting

Phase 3.5: strategy and dataset fingerprinting

strategy_fingerprint hashes a strategy class's literal source text
(inspect.getsource), so two different implementations -- or the same
one edited after being validated -- never share a fingerprint.
dataset_fingerprint hashes each bar's (symbol, ts_close, OHLCV, feed)

subject: Phase 3.4: CPCV paths and probability of backtest overfitting
task:
Phase 3.4: CPCV paths and probability of backtest overfitting

run_cpcv (Part B): scores every C(n_groups, k_test) raw CPCV split's test set
via shu.research.blocks.sharpe_over_blocks -- never a single flattened backtest,
because a split's test set is the union of k_test groups which, for k_test >= 2,
need not be adjacent, so its bar indices can have the same kind of real temporal
gap walk-forward's rolling-mode fold unions can. Empirically confirmed on the
n_groups=6, k_test=2 default: 10 of the 15 raw splits have a non-adjacent test
set (a real gap), so this is the common case, not an edge case. Scope note
documented in the module docstring: this computes one Sharpe per raw split
(len(path_sharpes) == C(n_groups, k_test), 15 for the defaults), not the fuller
5-reconstructed-path CPCV the architecture spec and literature describe -- a
deliberate, documented scope reduction for this task.

probability_of_backtest_overfitting (Part C): CSCV over an already-computed
S-subsets x M-configs performance matrix -- no bars, no strategy, self-contained.
For each of the C(S, S//2) train/test partitions of the S subsets, finds the
config with the best mean train-half performance and checks whether that same
config's out-of-sample rank among all M configs falls in the bottom half.

k_test >= 2 can be non-adjacent, so a split's test indices can have the same kind

into shu.research.blocks (contiguous_runs, sharpe_over_blocks) and refactor
walkforward.py to call it instead of maintaining a second copy.

subject: Phase 3.3: prevent _aggregate_sharpe from splicing bars across a rolling-mode purge gap
task:
Phase 3.3: prevent _aggregate_sharpe from splicing bars across a rolling-mode purge gap

_aggregate_sharpe previously ran one backtest over the flattened union of every
fold's train (or test) indices. That's correct only when the union is a single
contiguous block (true for anchored mode, and rolling mode with label_horizon=0).
Rolling mode with label_horizon>0 purges label_horizon bars off the right edge of
each fold's own train window, opening a real gap between consecutive folds' train
windows -- flattening across that gap spliced bar N to bar N+label_horizon+1 as if
temporally adjacent, silently blending pre-/post-gap prices in any strategy that
carries state across bars (e.g. MovingAverageCrossover's rolling close window).

Fix: split the index union into maximal contiguous runs (_contiguous_runs), run one
independent fresh-strategy backtest per run, and pool the resulting *returns* (never
raw bars) before scoring one Sharpe. Degenerates to the previous single-backtest
behavior when the union is already one contiguous block, so both control tests'
numbers are bit-for-bit unchanged (confirmed by direct re-run). New regression test
uses anchored=False with label_horizon=100 to exercise the multi-block path, and
checks run_walk_forward's is_sharpe against two independent reference computations
(one per-block/pooled, one spliced) that provably disagree with each other.

subject: Phase 3.3: walk-forward analysis and efficiency ratio
task:
Phase 3.3: walk-forward analysis and efficiency ratio

run_walk_forward slices bars into each purged fold's in-sample/out-of-sample
windows (shu.research.splits.walk_forward_splits), runs a fresh strategy
instance through run_backtest on each side, and reports per-fold plus pooled
Sharpe (concatenating each side's daily returns across folds, not averaging
per-fold Sharpes -- more robust to folds with too little data to score alone).
WalkForwardResult.efficiency = oos_sharpe / is_sharpe, clamped to 0.0 when
is_sharpe <= 0.

Verified empirically against the two synthetic control cases: a genuine
stationary edge (trending_bars) generalizes (efficiency 1.12), a strategy
grid-searched against one noise series (noise_bars) collapses out of sample
(efficiency 0.016).

task:

Three branches merged clean, but each was written without sight of the other
two. These are the defects and gaps that only exist in the space between them.

An organizer could rewrite a member's comment. The UPDATE policy on
post_comments has to admit organizers so they can tombstone one, and row-level
security is per row rather than per column, so nothing stopped the body being
changed. §6.1 grants organizers "delete anyone's comment" and nothing more.
Being misquoted in a community where people see each other at jumu'ah is worse
than being unheard, and worse than the shadow banning §6.4 rules out. Postgres
cannot express a per-column policy, so a trigger enforces it, and a test now
asserts the denial rather than trusting the data layer to call the right update.

Removing a post or a comment left no audit trail. §6.4 requires every
moderation action to write to the append-only log, but record_moderation_action
is deliberately un-granted so only a SECURITY DEFINER function can reach it,
and the posts data layer had no such function to call. Neither branch could
close this alone: one owns the content, the other owns the log. Soft-delete and
the log entry now happen inside one function, so a removal cannot be recorded
in the content table without also being recorded in the log. An audit trail you
can forget to write is not an audit trail.

That split deleteComment in two, because the same word covered two different
acts. An author retracting their own comment is not moderation and is not
logged; an organizer removing someone else's is both. The caller now says which
it is.

A muted member met a bare database rejection. The mute is enforced in the
comment policy, but the composer had no way to explain itself — the posts
branch had no mutes table to read and left a TODO. The banner and the in-place
composer notice are now wired to the viewer's own mute, so the member is told
what §6.4 requires them to be told: the community, the expiry or "until an
organizer lifts it", and the reason verbatim, never who did it.

The posts branch also carried two local shims — its own isActiveMember and a
string-compare role check written to survive either side of the admin →
organizer rename. Both are replaced by the shared, typed helpers now that the
rename has landed.

Adds the five assertions that could only be written after integration: the
comment-body trigger in both directions, and the three §8.2 minimums about
mutes that needed the moderation table to exist. Seven todos remain, all of
them messaging.

Also stops the linter walking into .claude/worktrees — it is a copy of this
repo, and every file was being reported three times.

subject: fix: escape search terms in PostgREST or() filters
task:
fix: escape search terms in PostgREST or() filters

The directory search box was interpolated straight into an or() expression,
which PostgREST parses by splitting on commas and parentheses. Searching for a
name or a city containing a comma returned PGRST100 and a 400 -- the workhorse
screen of the app, broken by ordinary input. A crafted term could also append
filter clauses of its own; RLS still held, but the results were not what the
query intended.

Wrapping the value in double quotes is PostgREST's documented way to make those
characters literal. Verified against the live API before and after.

Wildcards are stripped rather than escaped: ilike has no ESCAPE clause over the
REST interface, so a literal percent sign cannot be expressed, and silently
widening someone's search is worse than ignoring a character they almost
certainly did not mean as a wildcard.

searchCommunities already had an ad-hoc version of this fix, stripping the same
characters and losing the match in the process. Both call sites now share one
helper.
